page.title: Overview
page.intro:
Some AI companies write down how their models should behave, in a document we call an **AI constitution**. As such, it is the nearest thing to a **rulebook** of model behaviour accessible to the public, which enables third parties to review it and test the adherence of the models to these publicly stated principles. We think **every company** that builds these models should publish one, answer for what it says, and govern it properly. [More on why it matters](/about#why).

We have gathered every constitution published as of October 2026, and you can read each in full in the [doc reader](/doc-reader/), passage by passage, with guidance to identify specific model behaviours. [Content](/index) looks at **the document**: how clearly it settles conflicts between its own rules, and how deeply it covers the behaviours a model should follow. [Process](/index?view=governance) looks at **the company**: what it publishes about its constitution, and how far it holds its models to it.[1](#ovw-note-1) [How we score](#ovw-methodology).

sections.title: Methodology
blocks: Each of ten companies gets two scores. **Content** reads its constitution, the document in which it says how its models should behave. **Process** reads what it publishes about how it governs that document. Neither score tests how the models behave. A constitution that covers a behaviour thoroughly is no evidence that the model follows it, and measuring that is work the index has yet to do.

blocks.title: How Content is scored
blocks: Content is the average of the clarity of the document and its behaviour coverage, each counting for half. A company that publishes no constitution scores 0 on every row. The figures come from a panel of three judges, each a frontier language model from a different company, which read the constitutions against precise written definitions. Each figure is the mean of the three judges, except where this section says otherwise.

There is no agreed standard yet for what makes a good constitution, and the index is a first attempt at one. It prefers a document that states its rules, and which of them wins, explicitly, because that is what lets anyone test a model against it. A document that deliberately leaves more to the model's judgement scores lower, and a clearer document is not proof of a better model. That preference is ours and open to challenge.

**Behaviours.** The index asks about fourteen behaviours in four categories: autonomy, oversight and authority; harm and safety; helpfulness and judgement; honesty and epistemics. Each is written in two parts, what it requires and where it stops, so that a careful reader could mark every passage of a constitution that bears on it. The behaviours, their definitions and their categories are the index's own, and open to challenge.

**Passages.** Each judge reads the whole constitution against one behaviour and gives every paragraph 3, 2, 1 or 0. A passage is kept when the three verdicts add up to 4 or more, and the sum places it in one of three bands. A defining passage is the document's fullest statement of the behaviour, a core passage establishes it, and a related passage bears on it without establishing it.

**Depth.** In a second pass each judge reads the kept passages of all three bands, with the passages that state the document's general rules for conflicts, and gives the behaviour a depth from 0 to 10. A depth is a reading of those passages and not of the whole document, so a figure can move when a passage changes band. The six levels sit on the even numbers. An odd number means the level below is fully met and the one above only in part.

- **0, absent.** Nothing in the document bears on the behaviour.
- **2, named.** The behaviour is mentioned, usually inside a list or a passage about something else, and nothing further is said about it.
- **4, discussed.** The document takes the behaviour up in its own right and says what it expects and why, in terms too general to grade an answer against.
- **6, prescribed.** The document states concrete do and don't rules, precise enough that anyone testing a model could quote its own sentences as the standard.
- **8, demonstrated.** The rules come with worked cases showing the response the document sanctions, close enough to settle a borderline answer.
- **10, bounded.** Demonstrated, and for every part of the behaviour the document shows where the line falls, names one of its own rules that pulls against this one and says which prevails, and says what to do when the case cannot be decided.
A behaviour's figure is the mean of the three depths. A category is the average of its behaviours, and behaviour coverage is the average of all fourteen, each counting the same.

**Clarity of the document.** Each judge reads the whole document and scores five criteria from 0 to 4, against written descriptions of what earns 0, 2 and 4, with a 1 or a 3 falling between the descriptions either side. Clarity is the average of the five.

- **Clarity when two rules are contradictory.** What the document says, in general, when two of its own rules conflict. A 4 needs a strict order that decides who wins, a rule for two rules of the same rank, and examples of the order applied.
- **How firm each rule is.** Whether a reader can tell, for each rule, if it is absolute or a default, and who may change it.
- **Reasons for the rules.** Whether the rules say why they exist, specifically enough to decide a case the document does not show.
- **Domains covered.** Whether the document has rules of its own for six domains: ordinary conversation, actions taken with tools, images, audio and video, users who may be under eighteen, other AI agents, and deployments a business has customised. The six are our list.
- **Remaining unsettled contradictions.** No judge scores this one. Each judge lists every contradiction it finds, every judge then reads every claim, and a claim is confirmed when at least two readings say it holds. None confirmed earns 4, one or two earn 2, and three or more, or any that involves a rule the document calls absolute, earn 0.

**When a judge cannot answer.** If a judge's provider withholds its reply, or its reply cannot be read, another model declared in advance judges in its seat. Each substitution is recorded with its reason, and the doc reader names the substitute.

**Provisional readings.** A constitution the panel has not yet read can be read provisionally by one language model, answering in one working session the questions the panel's judges are asked, through the same pipeline. Its passages, depths and criteria are one model's reading, and the doc reader marks them provisional. The panel's reading replaces it once the panel has read the document.

**Corrections by hand.** A passage's band, a depth or a criterion can be set by hand where the judges' figure is found wrong, with a written reason. The judges' own figures are kept beside each correction, and the doc reader says where a band or a depth was set by hand. As of October 2026, eleven behaviour figures and four criteria are set by hand. The depths raised by hand rest on worked examples, which the judges' rubric counts as related at most, so three judges can never keep one and the depth judges never see it.

blocks.title: How Process is scored
blocks: Process is the average of Transparency and Applicability, each counting for half. It draws on two working papers, and each part below says which one it comes from. The first is Polaris Collective's "Model spec governance and transparency: the state of play and four transparency asks", in its draft of 10 September 2026. The second is "Emerging International Best Practices for AI Model Specs" by Edward Kembery et al., a working paper under review.

**Transparency.** Eleven rows, each counting the same: the ten checks of five questions, and one practice. The five questions come from Polaris Collective's paper, and their checks rest on its text. The questions follow its four asks, with the fourth, on hard constraints, split in two. Each check is scored from 0 to 4 against a written description of what earns 0, 2 and 4, and a 1 or a 3 falls between them.

- **Published constitution.** Constitution published, coverage stated, and covers government and defence models. It is the paper's first ask.
- **Change log.** Versions kept, changes explained, and the scope of the log. It is the second ask.
- **Guardrails.** Guardrails disclosed, and guardrail changes logged. It is the third ask.
- **Hard constraints.** Hard constraints listed. No ask in either paper is behind this check. It uses the paper's definition of a hard constraint, and the fourth ask presumes such a list, since nobody can comment on the weakening of a rule that was never named.
- **Public input.** A window for public comment before a hard constraint is weakened. It is the fourth ask.
- **Open licence.** Anyone may freely reuse the published constitution. This row is a practice from the paper by Edward Kembery et al., scored 0, 1 or 2.
**Applicability.** Nine practices, each scored 0, 1 or 2 and counting the same. All nine come from the paper by Edward Kembery et al.

- **Four anyone can check from public sources.** Adherence tests published, outside testers, release threshold, and change approval published.
- **Five nobody outside a company can see.** Trained to follow it, internal models, same text inside, monitored in use, and separate sign-off. The paper asks companies to state the first four publicly and raises the fifth as an open problem. Each is scored on what the company publishes.
The paper describes no score for a practice. In ours, 2 is the practice in full, 1 is part of it or a weaker form of it, and 0 means we found nothing published.

**What is ours.** Neither paper splits a question into checks, weighs one row against another or says what earns a score. The split of each question into checks is ours, and so are the descriptions of what earns 0, 2 and 4 on a check, the summary of what 0, 1 and 2 mean on a practice, the weights, and the rules described below. The check that hard constraints are listed is ours too, as no ask in either paper is behind it, and so is the choice to score a separate sign-off on changes on what a company publishes, which the paper raises without asking anyone to publish.

**How the rows were scored.** The rows were scored by hand from public documents between 18 and 21 September 2026, and read again on 23 and 24 September 2026, when the passage behind each score was recorded with its address and date. On 25 September 2026 an audit carried out with language models checked every row against its sources. Corrections a second model confirmed were applied, and those held back were decided by a person on 26 September 2026. Ten rules settle cases the descriptions left open, nine written on 26 September 2026 and one on 28 September 2026, and apply to every company. One company, added on 28 September 2026, was researched and scored by a language model against the same descriptions and rules. No score was taken from another ranking. A 0 means we looked and found nothing public, and a company may follow a practice without saying so.

blocks.title: How grades are read
blocks: Every score that adds up other rows is a letter, read from its figure out of 10 as the page shows it, to one decimal. Opened, a cell shows the figure behind its letter.

- **A** from 9.3 and **A-** from 9.0. Meets nearly all of what the row asks.
- **B+** from 8.7, **B** from 8.3 and **B-** from 8.0. Meets most of it, with gaps.
- **C+** from 7.7, **C** from 7.3 and **C-** from 7.0. Falls short in places.
- **D+** from 6.7, **D** from 6.3 and **D-** from 6.0. Falls well short.
- **E** from 4.0. Meets about half at best.
- **F** from 2.0. Meets little of it.
- **G** from 0. Meets almost nothing, or nothing published.

Down to D, a minus marks the bottom of a band and a plus its top. Below D the scale runs in three bands of 2 with neither, because most scores fall there. A row scored directly keeps its own scale, 0 to 4 for a criterion or a check, 0 to 2 for a practice and 0 to 10 for a behaviour. Where rows are averaged, each counts as its share of 10, so a check of 3 out of 4 counts as 7.5.

**Overall grade.** The average of Process and Content, read on the same scale. A company with an F or a G on either gets no more than F, whatever the average, because a company that fails one score cannot make up for it with the other. An asterisk marks a grade held at F. Companies are listed by overall grade, and within one letter by the figure behind it.

blocks.title: For context
blocks: Two rows in the grid count towards no score and show what is at stake.

- **Capabilities.** The company's own model that scores highest on Epoch AI's Epoch Capabilities Index, which combines more than fifty benchmarks into one scale of general capability, shown as how many months it trails the most capable model Epoch rates. The months are our own conversion of the gap in points, at the 14 points a year Epoch finds the frontier has gained. It measures capability on benchmarks and says nothing about danger, and a gap of a few months is within Epoch's margin of error. The data are as of 28 September 2026.
- **Model usage.** Our rough estimate of how widely the company's models are used, from none to three filled figures, pieced together from the user counts companies state, developer traffic, downloads of open models and outside estimates. Much of what a robust scale would need is not public, and the kinds of use it combines have no common measure.

blocks.title: Limitations
blocks:
- **Judges reading their own company's document.** Two of the three judges are made by companies the index scores, and each reads its own company's constitution. The models behind the provisional readings, the figures set by hand and the audit of the Process rows are also made by a company the index scores. Nothing in the figures corrects for this. In the audit, corrections that would have raised that company were held until a person decided them.
- **Readings by one model.** A provisional reading is one model's, and the model that finds a contradiction also confirms it, where the panel needs two readings of three. Each figure set by hand was read from the document by one reader, a language model. As of September 2026, no person has read the Process rows a language model scored against their sources.
- **Contradictions.** The last criterion of clarity turns on what the judges happen to notice in one reading, and it can swing its whole range between two runs over the same text. As of September 2026, no person has reviewed a contradiction the judges confirmed.
- **Depth reads what was kept.** A behaviour the judges cited thinly is scored on what they cited. Two behaviour figures were restored by arithmetic from stored values.
- **Scores that are ours.** Every Process score, and the checks, weights, descriptions and rules behind it, are ours and follow no established scoring method. A different reading could move a company by a few points.
- **Downloadable models.** No Process question reaches how a model behaves once someone has downloaded it, so for a company whose flagship model anyone can download, part of a low score reflects a limit of the questions.
- **What could not be checked.** Some pages carry no date and have no earlier copy, so a quiet edit to them would not show. The Chinese regulatory filings could not be retrieved. One constitution serves no text at its own address, so it is read from the index's own copy. It is published in Chinese and read in an English translation, and the doc reader shows the original beside every passage.
### Where to read more

[About](/about) explains why constitutions matter and how to propose a constitution or a behaviour. The [doc reader](/doc-reader/) shows every passage behind a behaviour figure, why it was cited and how strongly, and the depth each judge gave. The Index pages, [Content](/index) and [Process](/index?view=governance), set out what earns each score on every criterion and check, and Process lists the sources it read for each company.

sections.title: Sources reviewed
blocks: What was read for each company, with the address of each document. The last group holds the sources that cover more than one company. Each document carries the code the texts on this page cite it by, and the passages we quote from it. The sources of the context rows close the list.

grid.caption: The overall grade of ten companies and the two final scores of the index it averages, each a letter from A to G, each final score opening into the rows it is made of

overall.name: Overall grade
overall.plain: The average of the two final scores, Process and Content, each a figure out of 10, read on the same scale as every other letter. A company with an F or a G on either cannot get more than F.

rows.name: Transparency
rows.plain: Whether the company publishes a constitution for its models, how transparently it records its changes, its guardrails and hard constraints, whether the public can comment on it before it changes, and whether its licence lets anyone reuse it.

rows.name: Applicability
rows.plain: What the company says about training its models on the constitution, testing them against it and controlling changes to it.

final.plain: What the company publishes about its constitution and how far it binds its models to it.

rows.name: Clarity of the document
rows.plain: How clearly the constitution says which rule wins when two conflict, how firm each rule is, whether its rules give the rationale behind them, which specific domains have context-specific rules of their own, and whether the document contradicts itself.

rows.name: Behaviour coverage
rows.plain: How deeply the constitution addresses fourteen behaviours a model should follow.

final.plain: The clarity of the document and its behaviour coverage.

grid.scale: Every score is **a letter**, read from the figure out of 10 the Index gives: **A from 9.3, B from 8.3, C from 7.3 and D from 6.3**, then **E from 4.0, F from 2.0 and G from 0**. A minus marks the bottom of a band and a plus its top: A- from 9.0, B+ from 8.7, B- from 8.0, and so on down to D- from 6.0. Below D the scale runs in three bands of 2, because most scores fall there, and E, F and G carry no plus or minus. Press the key under the grid to see every letter and the figures it covers. The letter is read from the figure as it is shown, to one decimal. A cell, once opened, shows the figure out of 10 behind its letter. Opened, a score shows the rows it is made of: a row that adds up others is a letter on the same scale, and a row scored directly keeps its own scale, 0 to 4 for a criterion or a check, 0 to 10 for a behaviour and 0 to 2 for a practice.
grid.hint: Press a cell to see the score behind it, or the key under the grid to see the figures each letter covers.

grade_scale.title: The grading scale
grade_scale.text: Each letter stands for the scores out of 10 beside it.

grade_words.A: Meets nearly all of what the row asks
grade_words.B: Meets most of it, with gaps
grade_words.G: Meets almost nothing, or nothing published

grid.no_constitution: It publishes no constitution, so there is nothing to score here. A document of this kind may exist inside the company without having been released.

notes.title: Our ambition
notes.text: We are working on two more views. Regulation will follow how far laws and regulators refer to these documents and ask companies to keep them. Adherence will carry the results of independent organisations testing whether a model actually behaves as its constitution says.

name_notes.title: Held at F
name_notes.text: A company with an F or a G on either of its two scores gets no more than F overall, whatever the average of the two.

takeaways.title: Four of ten companies publish a constitution
takeaways.text: OpenAI, Anthropic, Alibaba and Microsoft AI publish one, and Microsoft AI published its Code of Conduct as a draft open for public comment that its models are not yet trained on. Google DeepMind, Meta, xAI, Mistral AI, Moonshot AI and DeepSeek publish no document setting out how their models should behave. However, such a document may exist internally without being released: Meta says it evaluates its Muse Spark model against one.

takeaways.title: Almost every company is weak on transparency to changes in their constitution
takeaways.text: No company's public change log says in full what it covers and how soon a change is recorded. None commits to warn the public before weakening a rule its model must never break, and every weakening we found went out without notice. For instance, in August 2026 OpenAI replaced a root-level requirement for "a shutdown timer" with "an ending condition", and its change log does not mention it.

takeaways.title: No company says which rules apply to governments and in military contexts
takeaways.text: We found no company that publishes the rules its models follow when they are deployed for governments or defence. Anthropic writes that [some models built for specialised uses do not fully fit its constitution](https://www.anthropic.com/constitution), and [a spokesperson told TIME](https://time.com/7354738/claude-constitution-ai-alignment/) that its military models may not be trained on it. xAI agreed to the Pentagon's "all lawful use" standard for Grok, [as Axios reported](https://www.axios.com/2026/02/23/ai-defense-department-deal-musk-xai-grok).

takeaways.title: Three companies have agreed to write this document for a regulator, and not for the public
takeaways.text: Google, Mistral AI and xAI publish no constitution even though they [have signed](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/contents-code-gpai) the part of the EU's General-Purpose AI Code of Practice ([Measure 7.1 of its Safety and Security chapter](https://code-of-practice.ai/)) that asks, for models with systemic risk, for a report on the principles a model follows, how it ranks instructions and what it refuses. That report goes to the EU AI Office and is not public.

takeaways.title: OpenAI and Anthropic lead on governance, and still fall short there
takeaways.text: OpenAI's constitution gets a B and Anthropic's a C, and on governance OpenAI gets a D- and Anthropic an E, the highest grades any company gets there. Neither keeps a complete public record of what changes in its constitution and when, neither publishes a full account of how its models are tested against it, and neither sets a bar a model must clear on it before release. Alibaba's constitution gets a B-, but it names none of the models it governs, and Alibaba gets an F on governance. Microsoft AI gets a D on its constitution, a Code of Conduct that is still a draft, and an F on governance.

openai.profile: OpenAI publishes a constitution, the Model Spec, that is explicit throughout: it ranks every instruction by who gave it and says how firm most of its rules are. It is openly licensed and keeps its past versions. The rest of its governance is thinner, with a change log that explains changes only in part, and tests of its models against the document published once, in March 2026, and not updated for its newest models.
openai.constitutions: A strong document on both counts. It settles conflicts by rank, leaves no contradiction unsettled and covers the behaviours in depth, most of all helpfulness and judgement, and harm and safety. Its thinnest area is autonomy and oversight, including concentrations of power and secret loyalties.
openai.whole: Full marks on three criteria and close to them on a fourth. Conflicts are settled by rank, most rules say how firm they are, every situation checked has rules of its own and no contradiction stands. Reasons are the gap: they run through the safety and privacy rules and are missing from several root content rules, such as intellectual property, extremism, hate and fairness, and from the formatting rules.
openai.behaviours: Deep on helpfulness and judgement and on harm and safety, with rules and worked examples, and nearly as deep on honesty. Autonomy and oversight is its weakest category, with little on concentrations of power and secret loyalties.
openai.governance: A little over half marks. The constitution itself is public, openly licensed and versioned, and the company says the public text, though it leaves out some detail, is consistent with the behaviour it trains its models for. Testing is thin: it published one set of adherence tests in March 2026 and has not kept it current, none of its outside evaluators tests adherence to the Model Spec, and no threshold decides whether a model is released.
openai.published: The Model Spec is public under an open licence, at a dated address with all its past versions, and says what it covers. The change log, the guardrails and the hard constraints are documented only in part, and it names kinds of deployment without saying whether government use is among those it governs.
openai.engages: Strong on use: it says how its public text relates to the one it trains on, and models are monitored in use. Training on the document is described in detail only for an earlier generation of models. Change control is partial. Testing is thin: one set of adherence tests, published in March 2026 and not kept current, outside evaluators who test other risks, and no threshold that decides whether a model is released.

anthropic.profile: Anthropic publishes Claude's Constitution, a long document that explains its reasons and covers the behaviours in depth, while applying the order of its core values holistically rather than strictly, by design. It is openly licensed, says which models it covers, and the company says its models are trained on it. It keeps no change log for it, and little is published on testing.
anthropic.constitutions: Deep on the behaviours and less explicit as a document. It covers harm, helpfulness and oversight in depth, but it applies the order of its values holistically by design, so it rarely says in advance how a given conflict resolves.
anthropic.whole: Its strength is reasons: nearly every rule says why it exists. It is weaker on which rule wins, on how firm each rule is and on the domains it covers, partly because it is written to leave room for judgement, and it leaves two contradictions unsettled. Images, audio and video have no rules of their own.
anthropic.behaviours: Deep on helpfulness and judgement and on harm and safety. Honesty and epistemics is its lowest category, held down by sycophancy and contested questions, and within autonomy and oversight it says least about secret loyalties.
anthropic.governance: A little over half marks. The constitution is public, openly licensed and says which models it covers, and the company says its models are trained on it and that the same text is used inside. The constitution has no change log, though its earlier version is still online and the company has committed to update the public text within 90 days of deploying a model trained on a newer one. Nothing is published on change control, and testing is thinly documented: a claim of adherence with no method, and outside evaluators who test other risks.
anthropic.published: The constitution is public under an open licence, says which models it covers and lists its hard constraints in full. Its record of changes is the weak point: the constitution has no change log and no version number, its 2023 version is still online with no link back to it, and nothing records later edits, though the company has committed to update the public text within 90 days of deploying a model trained on a newer one.
anthropic.engages: Strong on training and use: models are trained on the constitution, the same text is used inside and models are monitored in use. Nothing is published on change control, and little on testing against the document: a claim of adherence with no method, and outside evaluators who test other risks.

notes.whole: This row averages five criteria. Claude's Constitution chooses to rank its values and leave their application to the model's judgement, which lowers its figures on which rule wins and on how firm each rule is. It also has no rules for images, audio or video. We prefer clarity, because it is what lets anyone test a model against what its constitution says. That preference is ours, and it is open to challenge.

alibaba.profile: Alibaba's Model Spec is a well-built rulebook that settles conflicts explicitly. It is published by Alibaba's AI governance laboratory in the company's name, and it names no model it governs. Almost nothing is published about how it is maintained. Alibaba says it is training its models towards it, and its lab has built one research model on it and scored two Qwen models against it, neither from the current Qwen line.
alibaba.constitutions: A strong document. It is explicit about which rule wins between levels, its rules are firm and no contradiction is left unsettled, and it covers helpfulness and honesty well. Its gaps are reasons, which are brief and missing from its hard prohibitions, and autonomy and oversight, especially secret loyalties.
alibaba.whole: Clear about which rule wins between levels and how firm each rule is, with rules for nearly every situation checked and no unsettled contradiction. Reasons are its weak point: most rules give one in a single clause, and its hard prohibitions give none.
alibaba.behaviours: Deep on helpfulness and judgement, and good on honesty and on harm and safety. Autonomy and oversight is its weakest category, with very little on secret loyalties.
alibaba.governance: Low. The document is public and lists its hard constraints, though some are set by other policy documents it does not publish. It names no model it covers, though it implies that it governs Alibaba's production models, has no change log, and says it is open source without naming a licence. The guardrails of its own model platform are listed by category. Its lab has published scores against it for two Qwen models that stop before the current line, and nothing is published on who approves a change.
alibaba.published: The constitution is public and lists its hard constraints, though some are set by other policy documents it does not publish. It names no model it covers, though it implies that it governs Alibaba's production models, keeps no change log and says it is open source without naming a licence. The guardrails of its own model platform are listed by category, with no list for its apps.
alibaba.engages: A little on training and testing. The document says Alibaba is training its models towards it, and that its values match internal standards though the public text leaves out detail. Its lab has published scores against it for two Qwen models that stop before the current line. Nothing is published on monitoring or on who approves a change.
alibaba.caveat: It was published in Alibaba's name on the site of its AI governance laboratory (AAIG). It says Alibaba is training its models towards it and names none of them. As of September 2026, the only model we found publicly built on it is Oyster-II, a research model built on Qwen3-14B, and the same release scores Qwen3-Max and Qwen3.5-397B against it.

microsoft.profile: Microsoft AI publishes a constitution for its MAI models, the Humanist AI Code of Conduct, as a draft open for public comment that it says its models are not yet trained on. The Code puts safety and human control above its other objectives and lists ten constraints nobody can override. Around it little is published: no change log, no licence, and tests of one model against the company's own safety policies rather than against the Code.
microsoft.constitutions: A D, from a provisional reading by one model. The Code says which rules come first, safety and human control, and leaves clashes below that to judgement, three of which stand unsettled. It covers honesty in depth and gives most behaviours quotable rules with one worked case or none.
microsoft.whole: Clear on which rules come first and on the force of each part, with reasons for most sections and rules for every situation checked, images, audio and video only thinly. It loses most on contradictions: three clashes between guidelines of the same rank have nothing to say which prevails, which puts that criterion at zero.
microsoft.behaviours: Deepest on honesty, with rules and worked cases. Most other behaviours have quotable rules and one worked case or none, and preventing secret loyalties and avoiding concentrations of power are only named, in rules about other things.
microsoft.governance: Below half marks. The Code is public, lists its absolute constraints and was opened for comment with a promise to consult on new versions. It is a draft not yet in force, with no change log and no licence, and one of its models is tested against the company's own safety policies rather than against the Code.
microsoft.published: The Code is public and lists its ten absolute constraints, and its consultation is open to anyone, with a promise to consult again on new versions. It carries one date and no version number, change log or licence, its coverage counts only as implied while it is a draft, and its guardrails are listed by category for one platform only.
microsoft.engages: The Code is not yet used to train the models, and nothing is published on who may change it. The company tests one of its models against its own safety policies and gates each release on those tests, and outside testers have assessed its models for other risks.

google.profile: Google DeepMind publishes no constitution. What it says about how Gemini should behave is spread across several documents with different owners, and it describes the guardrails it offers developers in detail. It keeps little record of how these rules change, and its model cards test each current model against the safety policies they list.
google.governance: Low. There is no single constitution, a detailed account of developer guardrails and almost no record of changes to the rules. Its model cards test each current model against the safety policies they list and say each met a launch threshold for child safety, and it describes some outside testing, training and monitoring.
google.published: No single constitution: its rules for the Gemini app are spread across several documents, and its model cards tie its safety policies to named models. The guardrails it offers developers are described in detail. It refers to a set of harms that are always blocked without listing them, and keeps little record of changes.
google.engages: Its model cards publish tests of each current model against the safety policies they list, and say each met a launch threshold for child safety without publishing its level. It uses outside testers and describes some training and monitoring. Nothing is published on who approves a change to the rules.

mistral.profile: Mistral AI publishes no constitution. It publishes the system prompts of its coding agent, which rank instructions and mark a few as not overridable, with every change visible line by line, and it documents in detail the guardrails it offers developers. Nothing is published on training or testing its models against written rules.
mistral.governance: Low. Its points come from the system prompts of its coding agent, which the governance view counts as a partial constitution, with their history line by line and a short list of approvals marked as not overridable, and from the guardrails it offers developers. Nothing is published on training, testing or change control.
mistral.published: No constitution. It publishes the system prompts of its coding agent under an open licence, with every change shown line by line, and they mark a short list of approvals as not overridable. The guardrails it offers developers are well described, with some record of their changes.
mistral.engages: Nothing found on training, testing or change control.

meta.profile: Meta publishes no constitution, but has committed in writing to publish one. It says more about testing and training its models than about any written rules.
meta.governance: Low. Little is published about its rules, though it lists by kind the guardrails of its Muse agent, describes those it offers developers and announces some changes to its safeguards in its newsroom. It publishes adherence testing against an internal specification, and describes outside testers and training against internal policies.
meta.published: Little: no constitution and no list of hard constraints, a short record of versions of its framework, fragments of intended behaviour in a template prompt and rules for teenagers, and guardrails described for developers and listed by kind for its Muse agent, with some changes to them announced in its newsroom.
meta.engages: Some published adherence testing against an internal specification, outside testers, and training and monitoring against internal policies. It names who confirms changes to its risk framework and nobody for a document on how its models behave.

xai.profile: xAI publishes no constitution. The rules it has published for its models are system prompts for models it has since retired, and what it describes of its guardrails and testing is partial.
xai.governance: Low. It published safety prompts for models it has since retired, with a log that shows each change line by line, and gives partial accounts of its guardrails, announcing some changes to them on X. It acknowledges that government agencies may get fuller functionality, without saying what rules apply there. Its model cards test Grok against a refusal policy published only for those retired models, and an outside testing agreement has produced no published result.
xai.published: No constitution. A list of disallowed activities, marked as overriding every other instruction, was published for its 2025 API models, since retired, and its log of prompt changes, which shows each change line by line, stopped in November 2025. It gives a partial account of its guardrails, announces some changes to them on X, and says government agencies may get fuller functionality without saying what rules apply.
xai.engages: Its model cards test how often Grok complies with requests its refusal policy says to refuse, and it describes training and monitoring against that policy, which is published only for models since retired. It signed an outside testing agreement that has produced no published result. On change control there is only a 2025 statement that prompt changes need review, with no approver named.

moonshot.profile: Moonshot AI publishes no constitution: the nearest thing is a default system prompt in its developer guide. Little is published about its rules, how they change or how its models are held to them.
moonshot.governance: Very low. A sample system prompt, dated terms with no record of what changed, a description of the content filter on its API and in its app, and a 2025 red-team, tied to no behaviour document, of a model since withdrawn.
moonshot.published: No constitution, only a sample system prompt in its developer guide. Its terms are dated, with no record of what changed, and it describes the content filter on its API and in its app.
moonshot.engages: Almost nothing: a description of some training against internal policies. Its one published safety test, a red-team of a model since withdrawn, is tied to no behaviour document, and nothing is published on change control.

deepseek.profile: DeepSeek publishes no constitution. Beyond a disclosure page of the kind its regulator requires and its R1 paper of 2025, almost nothing is published on how its models are governed.
deepseek.governance: Very low: the disclosure its regulator requires, a contractual right to filter inputs and outputs, and a paper of 2025 that describes the safety training, the risk control system and a safety evaluation of its R1 model. Nothing of the kind has been published for later models.
deepseek.published: No constitution. Beyond the disclosure its regulator requires, there is its R1 paper of 2025, which describes its safety training and its risk control system, and the system prompts of two models, published in their 2025 model cards.
deepseek.engages: A description of training against an internal policy, and a safety evaluation of R1, a model it no longer serves, against its own standards.

context.name: For context
context.plain: Two things about each company that no figure of the index counts: how capable its most capable model rated by Epoch AI is, and our rough estimate of how widely its models are used. They are here to show what is at stake, and they change nothing above.
context.note: These rows show how capable each company's best model rated by Epoch AI is and roughly how widely its models are used. A published, well-governed constitution matters more as both grow. They count towards no score, and each cell says where its figure comes from.

rows.name: Capabilities
rows.plain: The model the company builds itself that scores highest on the Epoch Capabilities Index, which combines more than fifty benchmarks into one scale of general capability, shown as how many months it trails the most capable model Epoch rates. Epoch finds that the frontier has gained about 14 points a year on its index since reasoning models arrived, so we read a gap in points as that much time. It measures capability, not danger, and a gap of a few months is within Epoch's margin of error.
rows.source: Epoch AI, Epoch Capabilities Index, as of 28 September 2026
rows.what: The model the company builds itself that scores highest on the Epoch Capabilities Index, which combines more than fifty benchmarks into one scale of general capability, shown as how many months it trails the most capable model Epoch rates.
rows.from: Epoch AI's Epoch Capabilities Index, data of 28 September 2026, published under CC BY 4.0. The months are our own conversion, not Epoch's: we divide the gap in points by the 14 points a year Epoch finds the frontier has gained on its index since reasoning models arrived in September 2024.
rows.limits: It measures capability on benchmarks. It says nothing about how a model behaves or how dangerous it is. Epoch measures a lag as the time the frontier took to reach a model's score, which gives a few weeks to a month less for most companies. Models a few months apart are within Epoch's margin of error, so the order of the companies between 8 and 10 months behind should not be seen as significant. Epoch rates a model some weeks after its release and only the models it has tested, which for instance leaves out Microsoft AI's models.

rows.name: Model usage
rows.plain: A rough idea of how widely the company's models are used, from none to three filled figures. It is our own estimate, pieced together from chat assistants, API use and downloads of open models, and gives only an idea.
rows.what: A rough idea of how widely each company's models are used.
rows.from: Our own reading of scattered signals: the user counts companies state, their share of developer traffic on OpenRouter, downloads of their open models and outside estimates. For the number of people who use its models, we take the most recent figure that says what it counts and is less than a year old, whether the company states it or an outside firm estimates it. Where a company's only count covers one country, we also weigh its web traffic and its share of developer use. Each cell lists the signals behind it.
rows.limits: It gives only a limited idea of model usage. Much of what it would need to be a robust scale is not public. Most companies publish no comparable count of users, and the few figures for use through an API are counted in different ways. A chat assistant, a model called through an API and an open model downloaded and run elsewhere are different kinds of use with no common measure, so they may not be fully comparable on one scale.

capability.text: GPT-6 Astra, released on 3 September 2026, scores 166.6 on the Epoch Capabilities Index, within an interval of 163.0 to 172.0. Its weights cannot be downloaded. That puts it at the frontier: no model Epoch rates is ahead of it by more than Epoch's margin of error.

signals.text: OpenAI said on 6 August 2026 that 1 billion people a week use ChatGPT.

Its open model gpt-oss-20b was downloaded 6.8 million times from Hugging Face in the 30 days to 28 September 2026, a count of files rather than people.
